Total Inability
TOH-tul in-uh-BIL-ih-tee
n. phrase (Reformed soteriology; doctrine of total depravity)
From Latin totus (whole, entire) + in- (not) + habilitas (aptitude, fitness, capacity); the specific dimension of total depravity that concerns the fallen will's radical incapacity to seek God, receive the gospel, or do spiritual good apart from sovereign, regenerating grace.

See also: Total Inability

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Total inability is the Reformed doctrine that fallen man, in his natural state, possesses no spiritual capacity to seek God, believe the gospel, or do anything genuinely pleasing to God — not because he is compelled to sin externally, but because his will, mind, and affections are so thoroughly corrupted by the fall that he will never, of his own accord, turn to God. The question is not whether fallen man can do natural good — he can, restrained by common grace — but whether he can do spiritual good toward God. Jeremiah declares the impossibility: “Can the Ethiopian change his skin or the leopard its spots? Then may you also do good who are accustomed to do evil” (Jer 13:23). The change required is not moral reformation but the same order of miracle as a leopard changing its spots. Paul is equally absolute: “the mind set on the flesh is hostile toward God — for it does not subject itself to the law of God; for it is not even able to do so” (Rom 8:7). The fallen mind is not merely unwilling; it is not able. Ephesians 2:1 describes the baseline condition as death: “you were dead in your trespasses and sins” — a dead man does not respond to his surroundings. Christ draws the necessary inference: “No one can come to Me unless the Father who sent Me draws him” (John 6:44). The initiative must come entirely from God; the sinner left to himself will never come. This is why effectual calling, regeneration, and sovereign grace are necessary — not helpful supplements to human seeking, but the only operative cause of salvation. The 1689 LBCF (6.2–4) affirms this comprehensively.

Webster 1828 Definition

The specifically volitional dimension of total depravity: the fallen will's radical incapacity to seek God or respond to the gospel apart from sovereign, regenerating grace — grounded in Scripture's declaration that the natural mind is hostile to God and the natural man cannot receive the things of the Spirit.

expand to see more

TOTAL INABILITY, n. phrase. The Reformed doctrine that fallen man lacks any spiritual capacity to seek God, believe the gospel, or perform any act of saving faith apart from the sovereign, effectual work of God's regenerating grace.

Total inability must be distinguished from total depravity in emphasis: depravity concerns the extent of corruption (the entire person — mind, will, affections, body — is touched by sin); inability concerns the volitional consequence (the corrupted will cannot and will not choose God apart from grace). They are the same doctrine from two angles.

The inability is moral and volitional, not merely constitutional. Fallen man is not physically prevented from opening a Bible; he is morally certain never to respond savingly to what he reads apart from God's grace. He will not because he cannot, and he cannot because he will not — the two are inseparable in the fallen condition.

Common grace partially restrains the outworking of total inability in civil life, enabling unregenerate persons to perform acts of external righteousness, civic virtue, and ordinary justice. These acts are not salvifically meritorious, but they demonstrate that total inability does not mean every person is as sinful as they could possibly be.

The practical import of total inability is doxological: if man cannot take the first step toward God, then every step from initial grace to final glory is the work of God alone. Reformed doxology is structured by this impossibility — the glory goes entirely to God because the sinner contributes nothing but the sin that made grace necessary.

Key Scripture

Jeremiah 13:23 — "Can the Ethiopian change his skin or the leopard its spots? Then may you also do good who are accustomed to do evil."

Romans 8:7 — "Because the mind set on the flesh is hostile toward God — for it does not subject itself to the law of God; for it is not even able to do so."

Ephesians 2:1 — "And you were dead in your trespasses and sins —"

John 6:44 — "No one can come to Me unless the Father who sent Me draws him — and I Myself will raise him up on the last day."

Modern Corruption

Arminianism and semi-Pelagianism teach that fallen man retains a capacity for spiritual good — a “free will” that can respond to or resist grace — making human decision the ultimate determiner of salvation rather than divine grace.

expand to see more

Semi-Pelagianism, condemned at the Council of Orange (529 AD) but resurging in popular evangelical Arminianism, teaches that the fall has wounded but not killed the human will — leaving a capacity to cooperate with grace, to “allow” God to work, or to make the deciding move toward salvation. This is precisely what Ephesians 2 and Romans 8 deny. The fallen mind is not wounded; it is hostile. The fallen man is not sick; he is dead. A wounded man can cry for help; a dead man cannot. Semi-Pelagianism preserves human dignity at the cost of the sovereignty of grace and the necessity of regeneration.

Popular evangelical Arminianism (much of the American revivalist tradition) teaches that God has given every person sufficient grace to respond to the gospel — a “prevenient grace” that restores free will so that saving faith becomes a genuinely human contribution. The Reformed objection is not that God cannot give such grace, but that Scripture nowhere teaches it and its logic makes human decision, not divine election, the ultimate cause of who is saved. If man's response is ultimately decisive, then the glory of salvation is ultimately shared between God's provision and man's decision — a share the Scriptures never grant.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin totus (whole, entire) + in-habilitas (incapacity, unfitness); in Reformed soteriology, total inability names the volitional consequence of the fall: the will is not merely weakened but morally incapacitated for spiritual good apart from regenerating grace.

expand to see more

Latin totus — whole, entire; “total” inability means the inability is not partial or in one area only but extends to the whole spiritual person — mind, will, affections.

Latin in-habilitas — incapacity, unfitness (in- + habilitas, aptitude); the specific volitional consequence of total depravity, the radical unfitness of the fallen will for anything spiritually good.

Hebrew lev — heart; the Hebrew conception of the heart as the center of will, affection, and decision — it is this that is “desperately wicked” (Jer 17:9) and needs replacement (Ezek 36:26), not merely improvement.

Greek nekros — dead (Eph 2:1); Paul's image for the natural state is death, not illness. Dead men do not respond to stimuli; they must be made alive before any response is possible.

Greek dynami / ou dynatai — ability / is not able (Rom 8:7); Paul's language is categorical: the mind set on flesh is not merely unwilling but not able to subject itself to God.

Usage

"Total inability is the Reformed ground for evangelism, not the enemy of it: because sinners cannot come to God, preaching must be accompanied by prayer for the Spirit to open eyes — the preacher plants and waters, but only God gives the increase."

"It explains why conversion is experienced as new birth (John 3:3), not merely decision: birth happens to the person, not by the person — the sinner is passive in regeneration, then active in the repentance and faith that follow."

"Grasping total inability is the beginning of Reformed doxology: the Christian who understands that he was dead, unable to seek God, and that God sought him — that person has found the root of the hymn ‘Amazing Grace.’"
